newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Rubber pact seen more likely with EU agreement.
newsitem.headline: Rubber pact seen more likely with EU agreement.

text.p: The International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO) is confident of acquiring enough support for a new world rubber pact after the European Union's endorsement of the plan, an INRO official said on Tuesday.

"By the end of this week, we'll have a pretty good idea about the ratification of the INRA 3, and I don't think anyone will be holding out," INRO Buffer Stock Manager James Hegarty told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The INRA 3 -- International Natural Rubber Agreement Three -- is scheduled to come into force on January 1, 1997. It will be the world's only global commodity pact with economic provisions and a buffer stock that allows the industry to buy and sell rubber to stabilise prices.

Two cycles of the agreement -- INRA 1 and INRA 2 -- have been completed, but the third has been held over for a year due to delays in getting at least 75 percent of the world's rubber producers and importers to sign and ratify the plan.

The European Union said in a statement on Monday that its members had agreed to provisionally implement INRA 3. The EU decision, following that of the U.S. and Japan, means that countries representing 77 percent of world rubber imports have agreed to apply the agreement.

The INRO is the nucleus and administrative body of the INRA. It groups 23 major natural rubber consuming countries and six major producers and holds its all-important council meeting on Thursday and Friday.
Hegarty said the ratification was expected to be resolved by the close of the council meeting.
"I hope that by Friday, all will become much clearer," he said.
Industry sources said the new pact would sail through if Malaysia and Indonesia reached a compromise over the executive director's post in the INRO, which both were demanding.
Malaysia's Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik has warned that Kuala Lumpur may react adversely to the INRA 3 if not granted the INRO job.
Malaysia wants the top job in INRO under the pact, saying Thailand and Indonesia have had their representatives in the post under earlier agreements.
"We are among the world's top three rubber producers with Thailand and Indonesia. They've already headed INRO and we want our chance," Lim said during a rubber industry dinner last month.
Indonesia, however, argues that Malaysia already hosts the INRO headquarters in Kuala Lumpur and as such, the executive director's post should return to Jakarta.
